Honestly, I'm a bit torn. On the one hand, not commuting has given me back nearly two hours a day.
That's hardly trivial. But I'd argue we've lost something in terms of team cohesion.
I take your point. Spontaneous conversations by the coffee machine are surprisingly hard to replicate online.
Exactly. And for new hires it's even tougher — they're expected to pick things up without anyone to shadow.
Admittedly, that's a fair criticism. Having said that, I'm not convinced forcing everyone back five days a week is the answer.
No, that would probably backfire. People have got used to the flexibility.
What I'd propose is a hybrid model — say, two anchor days when the whole team is in.
That sounds reasonable, provided the days are coordinated. Otherwise you end up in the office on Zoom calls all day.
Ha, yes — the worst of both worlds. It'd need some discipline from managers.
Well, if you put it together as a proposal, I'd be happy to back it.
Great. I'll draft something and send it round by Friday.

lines.text: Good evening and welcome back to City Talk. Tonight we're discussing the council's plan to close the Old Town to private cars. With me is Pavlo, who has been cycling to work in Kraków for three years. Pavlo, are you in favour?
Broadly, yes. Anyone who's tried to cross the city centre at rush hour knows the current situation is unsustainable. That said, I have reservations about how it's being rolled out.
Go on.

Well, the ban comes into force in January, yet the extra tram lines that are supposed to compensate won't be running until the autumn. So for the best part of a year, people will have fewer options, not more.
The council argues that if they waited for everything to be in place, the project would never get off the ground.
I take the point, but sequencing matters. If people's first experience is of overcrowded trams and longer journeys, you lose public support, and that's very hard to win back.
Some listeners have written in to say the ban penalises older residents and people with disabilities.

That's a legitimate concern, and to be fair, the plan does include exemptions for drivers with a disability permit. But I'd go further: a door-to-door minibus service, at least in the first year, would cost relatively little and make a real difference.
What about businesses? Shop owners are worried that fewer customers will come.

The evidence from other cities actually points the other way. When streets become pedestrian-friendly, people tend to linger and spend more. Deliveries are the real issue, and that can be solved with fixed delivery windows early in the morning.
And cycling? Will it get any easier?
Only if the bike lanes are physically separated from traffic. Painted lines on the road don't make anyone feel safe, least of all parents with small children.
So if you were advising the mayor, what would your message be?

Keep the ambition, but delay the ban until the trams are running, and communicate far more clearly. People are much more willing to change their habits if they understand why and can see the alternatives.
Pavlo, thank you. After the news, we'll be taking your calls on this.
